newsitem.title: MALAWI: Malawi's fledgling multiparty system deadlocked.
newsitem.headline: Malawi's fledgling multiparty system deadlocked.

text.p: Malawi was mired in political deadlock on Friday, as it was the week before and the month before that. Politicians said the National Assembly, which ought to be in session, may not meet for an indefinite period.
"Right now, as I'm speaking to you, we have no agenda. The members have not given us the agenda, so we are not meeting," said the Assembly's Clerk, Roosevelt Gondwe.

Just over two years after the one-man dictatorship of Kamuzu Banda ended, Malawi's infant multiparty system began to break down in May when two opposition parties walked out of the National Assembly and vowed not to return.
Since the ruling United Democratic Front (UDF) party does not form a majority, parliament cannot sit.

The government has promised privatization of 26 state-owned corporations in 1996. So far there has been one -- an insurance company. Proceeds are supposed to go towards reducing Malawi's government debt.

Of a total 177 seats in the assembly, the UDF has 83 -- six short of a majority. The opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) and Alliance for Democracy (Aford) have 54 and 35 seats, with five seats to be filled in by-elections.

The two opposition parties quit parliament nearly six months ago in protest against President Bakili Muluzi's unilateral appointment of six opposition members to his cabinet -- without consulting their respective parties.
In the fiercely partisan press, charges of official corruption abound.
"We will not return to parliament unless the issues of our walkout are resolved," said Gwanda Chakuamba, leader of the opposition and vice president of the MCP.
But Muluzi has apparently made no attempt to reconcile the aggrieved parties.

Efforts by two public institutions, the Public Affairs Committee and the Malawi Institute of Democratic and Economic Affairs, to bring the three top political parties to the negotiating table have also failed.
Both opposition parties have accused the would-be mediators of favouring the government.
Repeated calls by the international community for the parties to come together have also fallen on deaf ears.

British High Commissioner to Malawi John Martin said Malawi's political leaders had resorted to the courts of law to resolve their differences, but doubted whether that could yield a solution to the deadlock, saying:
"My feeling is that you will not resolve political problems through the courts. There has to be dialogue."

The Malawi Congress of Trade Unions, the main voice of labour in the country of 10 million, has called for international intervention and threatened unspecified action unless the politicians resolve their differences.
So far there has been no apparent result.
